questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer:
First of all, I wanted to go abroad an experience other cultures. It was important to me to go to a place, where English is the first language. I considered both Washington, Edinburgh, Sydney, and Canberra as possible destinations. I also considered Tokyo, but that was with different expectations of my stay than if I went to ANU in Canberra. I chose ANU in Canberra as my first priority also because it is a part of IARU, which is why it was possible for me to apply for a large grand from The Novo Nordisk Foundation. Without this grant, it was not financially possible for me to go on exchange. Tokyo is also a part of this, which is why I considered this as well. 

Secondly, my girlfriend has lived in Australia and has a close connection to the place. I wanted to get to know the culture that she had lived in, so this was also a part of my choice. I also have heard from several people that Australians are, like Danes, laid back and humorous, which is also important to me. I went on exchange to get friends, not a cultural chock. Of course, looking back, there was some cultural chock, but at the same time, the locals around me have been very open and easy going.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
I have been feeling quite lonely for some of my stay and have struggled with my mental health for a long time before I went on exchange. It has been very challenging be alone on the other side of the Earth. I'm looking forward to being with my friends and family again. 

The academic experience was mixed as well, where I have several times seen lectures state things that are wrong or misleading. Also, during the semester I had either almost nothing to do or I had several assignments stacked upon each other or exams right around the corner. The semester felt very "back-loaded", meaning that almost all the work I did during the semester was in the last 4 weeks of it, where I personally handed in assignments worth around 60% of my final grades in total in the last 4 weeks of the semester as well as doing three exams worth 55%, 55%, and 50% each for each course in a span of 5 days, with only one week of studying before-hand, even though the exam period spans two weeks. Maybe I was just unlucky, but it felt unnecessarily hard. Also, the exam formats were not of good quality, and two out of three written exams had mistakes in them, which had to be corrected during the exam. The academic level was not as high as at University of Copenhagen, but the exams were very challenging, especially because of their formats, in my opinion.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: ANU themselves handed out a lot of information, and I was feeling very overwhelmed and missed some important stuff, because we got so many emails. My hall was helpful, but they were not very quick to answer. I had a lot of problems with my visa, but that had nothing to do with the university. Going to Australia is easy AFTER you've received your visa. I think that ANU was very slow, as they were only handing out acceptance letters in December/January. I got mine in the beginning/middle of January, meaning I had under a month to get my visa in place (I was flying out of Denmark the 5th of February). I got my visa 5 hours before my flight, even though I applied in mid January. For me, I had wished that they were quicker, as I needed only the acceptance letter to get several grant and visa applications going. I was ready for this already in the beginning of November, if I remember correctly. ANU did fail to - in time - tell international students when to arrive to campus. This information was given out only a few weeks in advance of the start of my stay, and I had bought tickets several months before this based on a more rough calender, stating that the semester started the 15th of February, where as the orientation and social weeks went on the two weeks prior to this. This was not known to me before after buying my flight ticket, which I did not buy excessively early.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I received a lot of help, when I arrived with small practicalities as well as general orientations. I wished I had gotten more social help, but that is more the responsibility of Bruce Hall, where I lived. ANU Global Programs has been extremely helpful throughout the whole process, both before and during my stay. They were very invested in my well-being and were available every workday of the week.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: Several. Both catered, non-catered. Mostly halls/colleges.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: The catered had no kitchens, most of the non-catered had big open kitchens, and some of the non-catered had studios with their own kitchens.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about on campus housing? *
questions.answer: If you are an older student (like me, 27), you can apply to live on Bruce Hall, Packard Wing, which is for post-graduates only. It is a bit less social, so if you are easily overwhelmed, this is a good place to go. For more social students, I would recommend living at Burton & Garran Hall, which is a cheap option with lots of exchange students (I was the only one at Bruce Hall, Packard Wing), Ursula Hall (catered), or Yukembruuk, which is more expensive, but also has a lot of international/exchange students.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I was not very satisfied with the social program at my personal hall, but I have told them about this and they are changing stuff to make it more accessible for international/exchange students coming to Packard Wing.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: You needed to apply for courses and they would respond with a yes or no, also giving a reason why. I had some problems, but it was a misunderstanding that was fixed in the end. They do not offer topics courses to exchange students, which I think is a weird rule that doesn't make a lot of sense to me.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Global Programs were available and also had a presentation on how to do this.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Semi-successful. I got many of the courses I wanted, but I did not get Special Topics in Statistics, which was something I wanted to do.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: I have none specifically.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I have already commented on this above.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA courses at your host university? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The level of the courses I took were of a good standard. There were some discrepancy between exam difficulty and course difficulty in some courses, but I expect that that is pretty normal, and something course convenors always have to adjust. For a university of this size, I would have expected higher quality of lectures. The lectures were all recorded. Some of the TA sessions were good, but it mostly depended on the TA themselves.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: It was more applied than at UCPH. Statistics and Computer Science at UCPH is also very theoretical. This made many of the courses easier to do, but on the other hand, when you are used to be taught with a bottoms-up approach, it can feel weird to be taught with a more top-down approach. Not all courses were like this, though. The exams only counted for around 50-60% of the exams, and the rest of the grades were based on assignments.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Statistical Machine Learning
Applied Time Series Analysis
Survival Models
Computer Vision

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I would recommend Statistical Machine Learning and Applied Time Series Analysis. They were good courses. The first is very theoretical compared to the other. The other two were not very interesting.

What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Many kinds of sports, hiking clubs, cave diving, social clubs of all kinds etc.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Depends on what you like.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Hiking, going to Sydney or Melbourne, going to Cairns for a diving trip.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Very easy, Danes and Australians are very alike

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Just be open and approach.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: None, really. The challenge was more that people already had friends and didn't need others. This is why I recommend going to other halls than I did.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The openness and laid back vibes.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Go to a social hall (BnG) 
Save money for trips
See as many people as possible

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Go. To. A. Social. Hall.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Meeting new people and developing personally.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Mental health issues and loneliness.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
